This paper introduces the Temporal-Varying Poisson AutoRegression with Exponential Moving Average weights (AR-EMA) model, a flexible framework designed to capture dynamic autocorrelation and seasonal patterns in count data. Unlike traditional AutoRegression models, which rely on complex selection mechanisms to manage high dimensions when the order exceeds two, the AR-EMA model utilizes EMA mechanisms to handle these dimensions efficiently. We demonstrate the model's utility through simulations and by analyzing monthly waste collection counts for 200 American cities. Findings reveal that the "September Effect," previously observed in specific cities, is actually a widespread seasonal phenomenon across all 200 cities, a pattern the AR-EMA model successfully captures. Additionally, aside from immediate short-term autocorrelation, long-term autocorrelation varies significantly by city and follows a U-shaped trajectory over a twelve-month horizon. The AR-EMA model offers distinct advantages over existing methods for modeling count data, particularly in estimating time-varying autocorrelation structures and identifying seasonal trends. These benefits make it especially valuable for business applications, economic forecasting, and public health interventions. Implementation details are available on GitHub at https://github.com/yaling1993/AR-EMA. Aerosol light contaminates optical measurements made with telescopes and plasmiometers intended for precision cosmology and climate science. To create maps of atmospheric optical depth ($\tau$) and column concentration (SCC), methods originally designed for stellar photometry—typically used to derive stellar parameters—have been directly applied without first validating the underlying assumptions. This manuscript evaluates these techniques to guide future assessments of both environmental monitoring and cosmological studies. Our analysis indicates that while this approach reliably orders regions or days by $\tau$ and SCC, it struggles to produce accurate absolute values, particularly when scattering dominates over absorption. Furthermore, deriving cosmological $\tau$ values from these maps requires calibrating the optical depth calculation, as the system is inherently blind to total light loss. Calibration is particularly challenging during clear-sky conditions, where conditions are most desirable for observing extra-galactic sources. Directly averaging local measurements to obtain global values introduces additional biases, and no existing method can directly observe cosmic stars under polluted skies without making unverifiable assumptions. Consequently, all current techniques rely on calibrated models or proxies (such as seeing, clouds, or stellar variability) to estimate global aerosol effects on extra-galactic observations. Similarly, deriving vertical optical depth ($\tau$) from solar concentration (SCC) measurements obtained by asembliers remains model-dependent, as direct observations are only feasible when stars are visible, which is precisely when extra-galactic studies face the greatest difficulty. We provide the necessary formulas for converting between $\tau$ and SCC under various definitions and illustrate these calculations using data from the European SuperSite network, DarkSky surveys, and DarkEnergySite projects. Additionally, we present a novel method to directly measure $\tau$ from cosmic stars visible through the Special DarkSky survey's optics; this method has been validated against DarkEnergySite and European SuperSite data. Ultimately, no current technique can directly extrat terrestrial aerosol light from extra-galactic stars to determine SCC or $\tau$ without additional assumptions or relying on direct profiling methods like those used by the European SuperSite, DarkEnergySite, and DarkSky initiatives. We introduce and assess a refined implementation of Langevin dynamics (LD) tailored for configurational sampling in molecular systems, addressing inefficiencies arising from anisotropic motion and collision frequencies. By calibrating the friction coefficient and integrating a revised velocity-rescaling scheme, we enhance sampling effectiveness, particularly in regions of high energy between degrees of freedom. Validation across simple models and a realistic lipid molecule demonstrates that this Rigid LD approach achieves efficient configurational sampling with friction coefficients up to five times higher than standard LD. Consequently, Rigid LD offers a robust, computationally inexpensive alternative to advanced methods like Hamiltonian MD or Bussi-rescaled LD, yielding superior sampling efficiency without introducing additional sources of statistical error. Furthermore, Rigid LD serves as a reliable foundation for accelerating dynamics through time-step enlargement or integrational improvements. This work provides the theoretical foundation, methodological framework, and comprehensive verification for OpenMM's constrained LD integrator, enabling its utilization in future simulations. In this work, we explore whether metadata from image descriptions on Flickr can be utilized to generate a probabilistic image-to-text mapping, serving as an alternative to relying exclusively on crowdsourced captions. This study presents a novel statistical approach to forecast the yields of additional baryons and mesons at the LHC, based solely on invariant mass spectra. Unlike conventional methods, which struggle with under-sampled regions in spectra, this technique initially models the invariant mass distributions of known particles—selected for their robust spectral characteristics—using flexible parametric forms. These models are derived from data and subsequently employed to estimate the yields of target particles whose spectra are undersampled or absent. The method was validated against invariant mass spectra of 21 well-established particles (including kaons, pions, and various baryons) produced in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV by the ATLAS detector. The resulting fits achieved high quality, with residuals remaining consistently low across all spectra and no significant systematic patterns emerging. Furthermore, the approach successfully predicted the thermal-like distribution of the $\Xi(2815)^{0}$ in the invariant mass spectrum of the $\Xi_{c}^{+}$, a relationship visible in data but difficult to confirm without this analytical support. Finally, the utility of this method was demonstrated by predicting the yield of the $\Omega_{c}^{+}$ meson from the $\Xi_{c}^{0}$ in the same dataset, where direct observation was not feasible. This flexible statistical framework provides a valuable tool for experiments operating in high-luminosity environments, such as the LHC, to determine the yields of rare particles. Such measurements are essential for assessing the baryon-over-meson yield ratio in hadron production and for investigating the validity of the statistical model of hadronization in particle collisions. A python implementation of this method is accessible at https://github.com/Atlas-TC/YieldPrediction. Key words: Hadron spectroscopy; Baryon production; Meson production; Statistical analysis; Particle yield determination.

This paper introduces SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents for the topic of integrated data and power wireless charging for single-input single-output (SISO), multiple-antenna input single-antenna output (MISO), and multiple-antenna input multiple-antenna output (MIMO) OFDM systems. Unlike previous equivalents focused on single-carrier integrated data and power systems, this approach utilizes an unbounded vector power spectrum density (VPSBD) formulation without requiring diagonal VPSBD as a constraint. Consequently, the need for OFDM carrier allocation to data and power streams is eliminated. Using this method, integrated data and power OFDM equivalents for SISO, MISO, and MIMO systems can be developed without assuming a fixed number of carriers for data and power streams. This flexibility offers significant advantages, including simplified system design, easier implementation, reduced circuit complexity, lower hardware costs, and easier upgrades or expansions. These benefits align with the goals of integrating data and power wireless charging systems, provided that OFDM benefits over single-carrier systems are maintained in the data stream. Numerical results from integrated data and power OFDM equivalents of wideband waveforming schemes for single-stream SISO wireless charging demonstrate that for specified charging rates, power backoff is unnecessary when using a direct current (DC) waveform. Conversely, achieving target rates with DC waveforms becomes feasible only when rates are sufficiently low. Finally, the advantages of combining multiple carriers and multiple carriers with multiple streams in integrated data and power OFDM systems will be examined.

Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) represents a complex Bayesian inference challenge that demands extensive computational resources and meticulous statistical management. While the Modernized Parton Distribution fitting framework (MODFIT) serves as a comprehensive environment for analyzing standard PDFs and exploring novel theoretical formulations, it operates above the level of an actual fitting framework. MODFIT integrates all necessary components, including data collection, data weighting, auxiliary functions, specific PDF implementations, integrations, convolution routines, additional theoretical calculations, the MODFIT intermediate language (MIL), the MODFIT C++ library, and the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) sampler (implemented via emcee). To facilitate the incorporation of new components, we have developed a unified theory framework known as FitterFramework (FF). This framework leverages the MIL and the FF C++ library, allowing external implementations to connect via the "FitterInterface" without requiring access to FF's internal details. Consequently, both MODFIT and FF utilize the most current PDF implementation, the MIL, and the C++ library, ensuring consistency across implementations. This document outlines the FF theory framework, describing its objectives, architectural design, and practical applications. Complementing this document, the "FitterFrameworkUserGuide" (UG) will detail the utilization of FF and its associated tools, while the "MODFITTheoryFramework" (TG) will focus on the theory aspects of MODFIT. Together, these resources aim to make MODFIT and FF as user-friendly as possible. The source code for FF, MODFIT, UG, and TG is available at https://github.com/MODFITCollab/MODFIT. We anticipate that FF will support a wide range of fitting projects, such as PDF analyses, Phenomenological Dark Matter models, Beyond Standard Model theories, Hadronic models like Hydrodynamics and Constituent Quark models, UV/IR models, and String theories. Furthermore, this theory framework can be adapted for projects unrelated to Bayesian inference, enabling the integration of any likelihood function for analysis, whether Bayesian or non-Bayesian.

This study presents a linearized model of a turbulent jet fire's response to acoustic excitation within an active flame configuration. Developed to simulate an oak tree fire impacted by wind, the model enables the investigation of flame dynamics under aerodynamic and acoustic forcing. While the base flow is defined linearly, external forcing is incorporated non-linearly. An optimization process determines the best-fit linear parameters for the airflow and gas-phase recirculation to accurately reproduce mean velocity profiles. Once calibrated, the model was validated against direct numerical simulation data, demonstrating high fidelity in predicting flow and flame characteristics across a range of forcing amplitudes and frequencies. Subsequently, simulations exploring nonlinear phenomena were conducted, including the examination of instability mechanisms driven by acoustic waves and the influence of forcing strength on flow structures. The results indicate that vortex formation remains largely unaffected by nonlinearity, as the flow consistently remains turbulent. In contrast, flame behavior showed significant nonlinear effects: at low amplitudes, fluctuations aligned with the jet exhibited standing wave patterns, whereas higher amplitudes triggered global oscillations. These findings offer insights into the nonlinear responses of jet fires to acoustic forcing and highlight the model's utility for exploring instability mechanisms in this context. Ultimately, this work underscores the value of linearized models for analyzing turbulence-fire interactions, particularly when detailed data for highly nonlinear systems is scarce. This research was conducted within the Europroject ACT (grant no. 771129). A video demonstration of the linear simulation is accessible at https://youtu.be/300400000.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a straightforward extension of Einstein-Cartan theory, characterized by a constitutive relationship between the constitutive tensor and geometric quantities, analogous to how material science links material tensors to strains. This study presents a systematic framework for analyzing NLG, detailing how to construct action, field equations, and energy-momentum tensors. We demonstrate that the nonlocal terms in the geometric constituents do not contribute to the local parts of the field equations. Consequently, the constitutive tensor must satisfy specific constraints to ensure that the energy-momentum tensor remains symmetric and satisfies the contracted Bianchi identities when derived from a NLG action. Under these conditions, the most general constitutive tensor is defined. Furthermore, we introduce a simplified formulation of NLG featuring an effective Weitzenbock constitutive tensor, where the nonlocal components reside solely within the constitutive frame field. In this approach, calculations are performed using a teleparallel geometry, treating the constitutive frame as a tetrad. We validate this simplified framework by deriving the most general constitutive tensor consistent with the previous constraints. Additionally, we establish the correspondence between this Weitzenbock-based formulation and the earlier general framework. Finally, we apply this methodology to the NLG of fluids, presenting the most general constitutive nonlocal Weitzenbock symmetric hyperbolic tensor.

This paper provides an overview of the most significant minority systems likely to be produced at the LHC, with a specific focus on their production mechanisms and expected yields. While this list is not exhaustive, it highlights systems that can be investigated via direct detection, reconstruction of decay products, or identification through vector boson fusion or forward activity. Although no single system will reach the statistical significance of "majority" systems like the $Z$ or $W$, these minority systems offer unique advantages: they provide ideal laboratories for precise standard model studies, allow for searches for new physics beyond current capabilities, and serve as excellent calibration tools for experiments. These yields were determined using PYTHIA8, with cross sections for individual processes often calculated separately with other programs before being input into PYTHIA8 to generate the total cross section and subsequent yields. The calculations assume an integrated luminosity of $30\,Ab^{-1}$ and an effective center-of-mass energy of $\langle s\rangle^{1/2}=5.01$ TeV for $p$-Pb collisions. Bipartite vertex splitting, a non-monotone graph transformation where a vertex is replaced by two connected vertices, serves as the inverse of bipartite contracting. Recently, Marx demonstrated that finding a minimum-size vertex contraction to achieve specific target properties is fixed parameter tractable (FPT) with a parameter of $\ell$ (the number of allowed splits) for eight common graph parameters $\xi$: clique width, cut width, separability width, elimination width, treewidth, rank width, tree depth, and twin width. In this work, we provide an improved FPT method for bipartite edge contracting (equivalent to vertex contracting in the complement graph) to satisfy various hereditary properties $\Psi$, extending Marx's result from $\ell$-vertex to $\ell$-edge contracting. Specifically, we show that for any constant $\ell$, a graph $G$ admits a minimum $\ell$-edge bipartite contracting to $\Psi$ if and onlyif its complement $\overline{G}$ admits a minimum $\ell$-vertex contracting to the closure of $\Psi$ under edge contraction ($\xi_{ec}$). Utilizing this approach, we establish further improvements: we prove that determining whether a graph can be made splitable, co-splitable, or a threshold graph through coarsening is also FPT with respect to $\ell$. Additionally, we demonstrate that for the parameter combination of twin width $tw_2$ and bipartite clique width $bcw$, the inequality $cliquewidth(G) \leq 3\cdot 2^{tw_2(G)+1}\cdot bcw(G)+1$ holds, which implies that deciding if a graph's clique width is at most a constant $k$ is FPT relative to $k$. Finally, we illustrate this method by deriving new upper bounds for the clique width of power graphs, distance regular graphs, and graphs exhibiting low bipartite elimination width. This manuscript is a revised and expanded version of our paper accepted at STACS 2020 ("A Fixed-Parameter Method for Bipartite Vertex Contracting and Applications"(arXiv:1901.09805), where the earlier method was described.

Extended degradation of CPU performance serves as a effective strategy to prolong the operational duration of battery-powered drones. This study introduces HyperDegrade, an automated framework that optimizes CPU throttling specifically tailored for real-time applications running on drones. Distinct from prior methods, HyperDegrade utilizes a compilation-time approach that considers an application's call graph and data flow dependencies to determine the maximum feasible frequency at each function without compromising task deadlines. The framework also accounts for thermal constraints and inter-task scheduling policies. Evaluations conducted on three real-time applications demonstrate that HyperDegrade achieves a 2.2x to 3.1x increase in end-to-end duration compared to existing energy management strategies, thereby extending the battery life of drones. The source code for HyperDegrade is accessible at https://github.com/SHARAD-INDIA-ICRE/HyperDegrade.

These games offer an engaging introduction to knot theory and have already been developed for knot diagrams, projections, and various equivalent representations of knots and links. We present a new unknotting game defined on welded knots and links, which is strictly more permissive than models based on classical knots. Consequently, our game falls between the operations of mirroring and crossing changes in terms of allowed movements. This shift in rules expands the potential unknotting procedures for classical knots and opens up new methods for wreathed knots. Utilizing this novel unknotting operation, we demonstrate that certain invariants previously thought to remain constant under crossing changes can actually alter values when these new moves are employed. As a result, invariants sensitive to the unknotting operation have now been established for classical, virtual, and welded knots and links. Furthermore, we introduce an unknotting value for knots and links, defined as the minimum number of unknotting moves required to convert a knot or link into the unknot. Through computational methods, we calculate unknotting values for specific (2,2)- and (3,3)-torus knots and several knot diagrams, including trefoils, Shimozas, and Figure-Four configurations, across all three categories. This paper introduces a multi-resolution tactical team of multi-agent systems (MAS) designed to maximize the informational value of a multi-agent surveillance mission. The approach involves low-resolution agents with broad coverage cooperating with high-resolution agents offering superior sensing but limited field of view. Both agent types operate independently without requiring direct communication. The low-resolution agents function as coordinators, dynamically selecting high-resolution agents to optimally cover high-information areas within their coverage. A Markov decision process (MDP) infinite-horizon model determines the optimal coordination strategy. Because the state space is vast, low-res agents utilize a novel lightweight neural network policy to approximate the ideal MDP decision-making. This method represents a significant advancement over current low-res MAS solutions, which rely on static mappings between high- and low-res agents. Efficacy demonstrations occur in both simulated environments and with a real multi-agent system consisting of Raspberry Pis and NVIDIA Jetson Nano devices. The results show that the proposed multi-res solution outperforms traditional low-res MAS approaches, achieving a 30% increase in information gathering. We present Cartesian Partition Method (CPM), a new technique for embedding a group $H$ as a quotient of the direct product $G_1\times G_2$, where $H\leq G_1\times G_2$. This approach derives a action of $H$ from the direct product $G_1\times G_2$ by partitioning the set of cosets of $H$ in $G_1$ and the set of cosets of $H$ in $G_2$ into identical collections. The resulting quotient map $\varphi:H\rightarrow G_1\times G_2$ is constructed by composing the action of $H$ on these partition sets with the natural homomorphisms $G_1\rightarrow G_1/H_1$ and $G_2\rightarrow G_2/H_2$, where $H_1$ and $H_2$ are the subgroups of $H$ corresponding to the two partition collections. Utilizing CPM, we present several examples of embedding discrete groups into free or wreath products. These results are potentially valuable for constructing counterexamples to address open questions in the theory of finite and discrete infinite group representations. The methodology and illustrations described herein are extended to the analysis of Lie group representations in a related publication. Mathematical classifications: 20F05, 20C15, 20H28. Enhancing the high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave sensors via alternative interferometer topologies has been considered essential for detecting astrophysical signals in the band of current detectors, which exceeds their nominal high-frequency limits. We introduce a novel configuration, termed the sloshing Sagnac interferometer (SSI), which utilizes the same optical chain as a Michelson interferometer but operates as a Sagnac interferometer above a specific crossover frequency. Within this "SSI band," the system functions as a dark-port readout Sagnac interferometer, leveraging amplification through parametric conversion. We evaluated the sensitivity of this non-linear band for the LIGO detectors and determined that a bandpass characteristic aligns well with the expected astrophysical signal profile in the SSI band. Simulation results indicate that the LIGO detectors' high-frequency sensitivity could improve by up to an order of magnitude within the SSI band. For LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA O4 and subsequent runs, this enhancement would allow the sloshing-Sagnac band to become the dominant sensitivity range for both LIGO detectors. Similarly, for the KAGRA detector, this new band would offer significant gains over its current high-frequency sensitivity. This paper introduces a stochastic medium access control protocol tailored for extra-large multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems. Distinct from conventional small-scale MIMO, XL-MIMO systems do not require round-robin scheduling for contentions-free operation, enabling higher throughput in contentionscenes. However, such scheduling remains viable only when all user visible areas (VAs) intersect, limiting its applicability. We propose a non-scheduled (NS) protocol for extra-largescale systems where VAs do not intersect, allowing simultaneous transmission without mutual interference between groups of users served by different access points. By integrating this NS protocol with a contention-based approach, we formulate an optimized problem to determine the most suitable protocol for each scene and derive the system throughput. Simulation results introduce a metric to evaluate the benefit of scheduling in XL-MIMO systems and confirm that the proposed protocol optimization yields significant throughput gains. Determining the meanings of words and expressions within specific domains or communities utilizes contextualized embeddings derived from large-scale corpora. While this method works well for established terms, it fails when applied to lexically evolving words, as the embeddings aggregate all contextual uses, including those that are obsolete, emerging, or pejorative. Consequently, pre-trained language models perform suboptimally on lexically changing terms, which are frequent in domain-specific and community-driven languages. In this study, we evaluate several contextualized models—BERT, RoBERTa, BioBERT, and Domain-BERT—alongside the semantically change-sensitive Semantically Enriched Language Model (SELMa), on three datasets: iSEC, MORDAT, and SLAT. Furthermore, we observe that contextualized models struggle to distinguish between different types of lexically changing expressions, a problem that does not affect SELMa. Based on these results, we propose potential directions for enhancing contextualized models when identifying lexically changing expressions. However, adopting an alternative approach for this specific task is both feasible and advantageous. We introduce the Quantum Relational Hoare Calculus with Expectations (QRHC-E), an extension of the QRHC that incorporates "expectations," a mechanism for asserting quantitative invariants drawn from quantum program semantics. Utilizing expectations enables the derivation of refined correctness proofs that are more precise than traditional relational assertions. Furthermore, expectations facilitate the formulation of expectation transformation rules, which allow for the reasoning about the invariant changes induced by individual quantum statements within QRHC-E. This paper defines QRHC-E, details its syntax and semantics, and presents a set of expectation transformation rules for quantum commands. The calculus supports a compositionality property regarding expectation transformation rules and an soundness property relative to the semantics of QRHC-E. Demonstrating the practical utility of QRHC-E, we apply it to prove the correctness of quantum algorithms for computing the inner product and Jordan measure, as well as a simple quantum circuit simulation language. These examples illustrate how expectations can enhance the precision of correctness proofs for quantum programs. The definition of QRHC-E with its extension points, along with the introduction of proof terms and an associated type system for QRHC-E, are reserved for the accompanying master document.

This study addresses the bias—manifesting as under- or over-densities—in the noise distribution of inversion algorithms used for vector magnetic field images of the Sun. While previous research suggested that the prior uniform distribution of noise within maximum entropy reconstruction (MER) algorithms is source of this issue, our investigations indicate that MER algorithms are actually effective at handling non-uniform noise distributions. The root cause of the observed bias lies in the assumption that the prior noise distribution matches the actual distribution of noise in the input data. To tackle this problem, we first evaluated the uniformity of noise in the line-of-sight (LoS) magnetic field distributions of LoS-vector inversion data (specifically, LoS-ionospheric correlation spectroscopy spectropolarimetric data). Subsequently, we applied this LoS magnetic field distribution as the prior distribution for the transverse magnetic field components within an ellipsical correlation inversion (ECI) algorithm when processing perpendicular components. As a final step, we utilized an anisotropic noise scaling (ANS) algorithm to determine the noise levels post-ecI-ECI. This approach yielded a significant reduction in noise, achieving an average decrease of 53% compared to using a standard constant noise level. Furthermore, the resulting noise distribution appeared more uniform and closely aligned with the actual data distribution. Although this method requires the LoS magnetic field distribution to serve as a prior for the transverse components, it represents a viable option when the statistical properties of this distribution are well-defined. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that an inversion algorithm's performance and associated noise distribution are not solely determined by the data itself, but also heavily influenced by the chosen prior distribution and its characteristic noise levels. Consequently, selecting an appropriate prior distribution is essential for obtaining an optimized and uniform noise distribution in the final reconstructed magnetic field vectors. To facilitate this, we developed a simple Python script capable of estimating the magnetic field distribution and its noise level from spectro-polarimetric data; this script, along with our analysis of noise characteristics before and after the LoS-ECI-ANS workflow using solar vector magnetic field data, is accessible at https://github.com/sharma-rupam/ANS_algorithm. For any group $G$, the collection of involutions closed under conjugation forms a union of conjugacy classes (UCC). In this work, we examine the boolean structure associated with the set of involutions in $G$, denoted by ${\bf I}(G)$, which consists of all elements within a UCC that can be expressed as the product of two other involutions in that same set. Focusing on simple groups of Lie type, we demonstrate that this boolean structure is necessarily trivial. Specifically, when $G$ is a simple group of classical type over the field ${\mathbb F}_q$, we establish the inequality $|{\bf I}(G)| \geq c_1 G (\log G)^{c_2}$, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are positive constants dependent on $q$. This result implies that the boolean structure of ${\bf I}(G)$ fails to capture the boolean algebra of size $2^{d}$ required for a $d$-design. These findings contribute to the investigation of $k$-designs. Additionally, we provide an algebraic characterization of the boolean structure for classical involutions of simple groups of Lie type. As an application, we prove that a complex of complexes of type $A_n$ satisfies the $2$-HAP (homological absolute purity) property if and only if it constitutes a complex of complexes of real involutions for a simple group of type $A_n$ of Lie rank one. Our analysis of the boolean structure of classical involutions also yields a solution to a problem concerning complexes of complexes of real invololutions for simple groups of type $B_n$. Furthermore, we determine the boolean structure of products of involutions within simple groups of type $C_n$.

This paper establishes that both special and non-special timelike Bertrand curves exist within $\nabla$-manifolds of arbitrary dimension, demonstrating that the characterization of special timelike Bertrand curves aligns with that of timelike spherical curves. As an application, the study defines and examines a new class of dual curves termed "special timelike Bertrand curves" within the dual manifold of the mean curvature operator. Specifically, the analysis confirms that a dual special timelike Bertrand curve is congruent to the special umbilical curve of the mean curvature operator if and only if its defining parameter satisfies a specific condition. It is concluded that a special dual timelike Bertrand curve is congruent to the special timelike curvature line of the mean curvature operator precisely when its parameter equals one plus the product of its curvature and sagittal radius. Finally, the study provides an example of a special dual timelike Bertrand curve in $\mathbb{M}_\ast^{2,1}$. For supervised classification tasks, the choice of loss function is a critical design decision that directly impacts model performance. Despite its significance, selecting the optimal loss function remains a challenging endeavor, as there is no universal guideline indicating which function best suits a specific problem. This study conducts a comprehensive evaluation of various loss functions for image classification. Our numerical analysis compares three widely used approaches: Cross Entropy (CE), F-beta weighted cross entropy, and Taneja's formula. Additionally, we introduce a novel metric designed to assess the performance of deep learning models utilizing these different losses. The experimental framework consists of three public datasets with varying levels of class imbalance: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and PLNLC-100K. Our results demonstrate that Taneja's loss function consistently outperforms both CE and F-beta across all experiments when measured by the F2 score. Conversely, the traditional Cross Entropy generally yielded lower accuracy relative to the other methods in this work. To further validate these findings, we added an information theoretic metric, the Kullback-Leibler divergence, to compare class probability distributions generated by the models. This analysis confirmed that Taneja's function produces distributions closest to the ideal uniform distribution for correct classes and the target fraction for incorrect ones, aligning best with the objectives of the F2 optimization goal. Ultimately, this research establishes Taneja's loss function as a superior alternative to standard practices, particularly for datasets exhibiting significant class imbalance, when the objective is to maximize the F2 score. The metric dimension of a graph represents the minimum size required for a resolving set, offering a measure of state space complexity useful in areas like robotics and networking. This study examines the metric dimension under the induced metric on finite graphs where the distance between adjacent vertices is set to one unit and is monotonically increasing for non-neighbors. We find that for certain graphs, the traditional metric dimension does not align with this new metric space dimension. Additionally, we establish upper bounds for the monotonically increasing metric dimension, which are always at least as large as the standard metric dimension. Our analysis focuses primarily on stars, paths, cycles, and "broom" graphs, which are constructed by attaching a path to the leaves of a star. Ultimately, we derive a general upper bound applicable to any tree.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for detecting heart abnormalities, yet its clinical adoption has been limited by the subjective nature of human listening and the high demand for specialized training. To overcome these barriers, automated electronic stethoscope systems offer a promising alternative. Despite the significant investment in cardiac datasets by research communities, these data resources have not been fully utilized to address the additive noise present in real-world clinical environments. This study presents a new framework designed to categorize heart sounds under noisy conditions without relying on noise pre-processing or estimation techniques. The proposed method integrates a convolutional deformation layer into a pre-trained noise-categorization classifier to learn optimal deformations for specific noise types. Subsequently, a conventional heart sound categorizer is applied to the "de-noised" phonograms. Experimental results conducted in a convolutional neural network environment demonstrate that this additive noise categorization approach outperforms standard convolutional networks. Furthermore, when tested on a dataset of real cardiac recordings, the additive noise categorization method achieved superior accuracy in detecting heart sound categories compared to a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network trained on real cardiac data. The overall contribution of this work lies in implementing an end-to-end automated system for analyzing real-world noisy heart sound recordings.

We demonstrate that for the ASEP with step initial conditions and particle number preserving boundary conditions, the velocity process of the traffic-ordered particles converges to a reflected Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process. Although this applies specifically to these initial and boundary conditions, it supports the broader conjecture that ASEP becomes a diffusion process under scaling limits. To achieve this, we must analyze the convergence of velocity processes across various initial conditions and prove that the limit is Markovian. This approach forms the basis of this paper. Specifically, we prove the convergence of velocity processes from any initial condition to a Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process and establish its reflection at zero. Additionally, we show the Markovian nature of the limiting velocity process occurs only when the drift of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process is one, consistent with ASEP's unit speed. Consequently, we derive the hydrodynamic equation from the continuity of the velocity process, confirming that the ASEP current matches the time derivative of the density. Finally, we extend these results to ASEP with generalized boundary conditions, assuming the Lindblad operator is conservative.

This study examines the various mathematical models utilized to forecast the progression of COVID-19, evaluating their respective strengths and limitations. Although compartmental models have historically been the standard for analyzing infectious disease dynamics, they have recently been supplemented during the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic by alternative approaches such as network, individual-based, and agent-based models. We provide a concise overview of these diverse methodologies, offering guidance on selecting the most appropriate framework for specific research objectives or epidemic control strategies. Furthermore, we identify key knowledge gaps that require attention in future investigations.

It remains uncertain why the star formation rate (SFR) of massive galaxies declines and why the shape of the specific star formation rate (sSFR)–mass relation is influenced by bulge properties. Using the ATLAS$^{\star}$9 dataset, we examined the properties of the most luminous Atlas galaxies, defined as those with $M_B < -21.1$ (\#LUMINOUS), and a control sample of Atlas galaxies just below this limit (\#CONTROL). We performed a Spearman rank-order correlation test between the sSFR and both bulge-to-total ratio ($B/T$) and bulge mass ($M_{bulge}$), splitting the sample by mass into two groups: $log(M_{\star}) < 11.1$ (\#LOWM) and $log(M_{\star}) \ge 11.1$ (\#HIGHM). Our results show that for the \#HIGHM sample, the sSFR correlation with both $B/T$ and $M_{bulge}$ is stronger than for the \#LOWM sample. Specifically, the correlation coefficient for sSFR versus $B/T$ was $0.21 \pm 009$ in \#HIGHM compared to $0.11 \pm 009$ in \#LOWM. Similarly, the coefficient for sSFR versus $M_{bulge}$ was $0.19 \pm 009$ in \#HIGHM versus $0.09 \pm 009$ in \#LOWM. Additionally, the median sSFR of the \#LUMINOUS sample ($0.0000034$) is significantly lower than that of the \#CONTROL sample ($0.0000051$) at the $2.7\sigma$ level. These findings suggest that bulge properties motivate the turnover of the $M^{\*}-SFR$ relation at high masses and that the bulge-driven turnover of the sSFR–mass relation differs from the behavior driven by spin. Consequently, when modeling the turnover of the massive end of the $M^{\*}-SFR$ relation, bulge properties should be incorporated, and the bulge-driven turnover of the sSFR–mass relation may serve as a simpler parameterization. This study presents a cross-lingual sentiment analysis model designed to transfer sentiment labeling capabilities from a high-resource source language to low-resource target languages. The proposed framework integrates three components: a multilingual sentiment classifier, a target language sentiment regressor, and an auxiliary classification task. Intended to function as a fully automated labeling tool for low-resource languages, the system requires only a small, manually annotated training set containing parallel sentences and sentiment labels. These findings confirm the feasibility of enabling low-resource languages with minimal linguistic assumptions and no hand-crafted rules, thereby offering a practical solution for deploying sentiment assessment across diverse languages on social media platforms. This study presents new constraints on the angular momentum evolution of low-mass classical T Tauri stars using high-precision, self-calibrated radio measurements for a spinning up sample of nine stars and an non-spinning up control group. The analysis confirms a significant distinction in rotational velocities between the two samples. Furthermore, it establishes a significant correlation between current rotational speed and the duration of prior mass accretion, as indicated by $\dot{M}$ upper limits. These findings support either angular momentum transfer via a disk outflow shock shock model for stars with high inferred accretion rates ($\gtrsim 10^{-8} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$) and suggests planetary ingestion for stars with lower rates ($\lesssim 10^{-8} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$). An alternative explanation involving planetary ingestion requires stars in this category to rotate significantly faster than currently observed, implying undetected angular momentum sources. Finally, the data rule out a simple torque model where magnetospheric alignment dominates and a constant torque depends solely on magnetospheric radius, particularly for stars with strong magnetic fields ($\gtrsim 120$ Gauss). If magnetic fields are coupled to the surface rotation, this result indicates that stars with higher rotational velocities must possess weaker magnetic fields ($\lesssim 120$ Gauss). Ultimately, the results align with a model where initial rotational velocity is determined by the radial location of formation ($R_{form}$) and subsequent evolution is governed by magnetospheric torque, with angular momentum gains from accretion dominating for $R_{form} \gtrsim 5-6 R_{Sun}$ and torques dominating for smaller radii. Additional support for this conclusion comes from a correlation between initial rotational velocity and the product of stellar mass and $R_{form}$ ($P_{acc}$) derived from a sample of 100 low-mass stars. While this model accounts for the rotational distribution of the sample, it fails to explain the spin distribution of the larger $ASs-2349$ star sample, indicating that further mechanisms, such as planetary ingestion, are necessary to match the observed rotational distribution of low-mass stars.

The global rise in fake news, compounded by the introduction of multimodal content like images and videos, has created significant challenges for detecting fraudulent material. However, the sheer volume and variability of unseen multimodal fake news continue to threaten the success of existing identification systems. This paper presents a novel approach for identifying emergent multimodal fake news using a meta learning framework. Specifically, we propose a task-oriented model based on Multimodal Emergent False News Identification via Meta Neural Process Networks (MOMENT), which integrates a modality encoder, a brain network, and a action classifier to detect novel fake news. The modality encoder leverages a pre-trained BERT model for text and a contrastive learning-based image encoder for visuals. The brain network utilizes a feed-forward neural network derived from the MOMENT model, while the action classifier employs a separate feed-forward network to decide between real and fake categories. Extensive experiments on two datasets, one containing 20 multimodal fake news posts and the other 39, demonstrates that MOMENT effectively identifies emergent fake content. Results show that this meta learning approach successfully determines whether unseen multimodal fake news is authentic or fraudulent, achieving an F1-score of 0.93 and an AUC of 0.94 on the dataset with 39 posts. These findings indicate that MOMENT outperforms both meta learning and learning based methods, providing a robust solution for identifying emerging multimodal fake news. The MOMENT framework is accessible at https://github.com/abhijit-1996/MOMENT-. We anticipate that this system will prove valuable for security communities, social media platforms, and end-users in combating misinformation.

Golay sequences find significant application in single- and multi-carrier communication systems, while their complementary properties have been leveraged in radar, sonar, and coding theory to enhance signal processing capabilities. Recently, these Golay complementary properties have drawn interest in optical systems, where Golay complementary sets of sets (GCSS) have been utilized to improve optical correlation techniques and increase capacity in code-division multiple-access (CDMA) optical code division multiple-address (OCDMA) systems. This report introduces new Golay complementary sets of sets (GCSS) constructed via the convolution and polyphase approaches. Specifically, we have developed a binary GCSS with lengths 9p² and 10p² (where p is a prime number greater than 3) using convolution and the polyphase method, as well as a binary GCSS with lengths 11p² and 12p² (for the same prime p constraints) through the polyphase approach. The feasibility of this construction is validated numerically for a length set of {99, 100}. Furthermore, we generalized the polyphase construction to create GCSS with lengths (9r + 1)p² and (10r + 1)p², confirming these parameters are feasible for any positive integer r. These constructions are achieved by selecting two auto-complementary prime sets (ACSPS) of length rp² and a set of two distinct GCSS sets with length (9r + 1) and (10r + 1), respectively, through the polyphase method. These set collections are then integrated with two ACSPS of length p to form a (9r + 1)p² and (10r + 1)p² GCSS set via convolution. Ultimately, a hierarchical construction of polypahse Golay complementary sets of sets (GCSS) is proposed, utilizing two GCSS sets of lengths (9r + 1)p² and (10r + 1)p² to create a (9rp² + r)p² GCSS. This final construction is demonstrated numerically for the length set {1782, 1980}, resulting in a 1,028,796 GCSS.

Segmental suppression lesions are an effective strategy for enhancing network segmentation performance and providing valid out-of-sample estimates. However, generating these lesions remains a significant challenge due to the difficulty of creating realistic artificial lesions and ensuring they remain segmentable. This paper introduces a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE) designed to produce segmentable segmental suppression lesions. Validity was assessed through statistical analysis, visual inspection, and comparative evaluation against other lesione generation methods. The PAVAE demonstrated higher realism and better alignment with real lesions than state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, it effectively preserved the segmentability of augmented images, exhibiting superior performance over alternative generation approaches. The practical value of PAVAE was verified by improving the Bayesian Probabilistic Network (CPN) with lesione  images, yielding statistically significant gains in test Mean Intersection over Division (MIoD) metrics for both medical and non-medical lesione images. The source code for PAVAE is accessible at: https://github.com/priyankhdevi/PAVAE.

Feature extraction via deep neural networks has been widely adopted in real-world scenarios, particularly when paired with student models to tackle specific tasks. However, existing methods lack comparability, making it difficult to select the most appropriate feature extractor for a given scenario. While DAE stacks offer one approach, they are inherently limited by their fixed, layered architecture. This paper introduces a unified framework grounded in comparative learning designed to learn any arbitrary feature extraction strategy. Initially, the system utilizes a collection of unsupervised auxiliary models through the comparative learning model to master the feature extraction mode. Subsequently, it guides the student model in addressing the actual problem. Empirical results from various datasets demonstrate that this framework outperforms traditional autoencoders and DAE stacks. Furthermore, the comparative learning model itself exhibits superior accuracy relative to other direct learning approaches within the same dataset context. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yy-chen/Unified-Structure-for-Feature-Extraction.

Large language models (LLMs) employed in real-world scenarios require a means to override inherent capabilities with externally provided knowledge. For instance, when acting as a chatbot, the model's native awareness of medical advice should yield to knowledge stating that specific topics are beyond its scope. This integration occurs at a structural level, where the graph representation of external knowledge is combined with the neural capabilities of the LLM. Consequently, effective ability-based knowledge integration is vital for this process. However, existing approaches—such as rule injection, RAG, and skill-based methods—cover only limited domains and fail to create a comprehensive, unified framework. Furthermore, current techniques often demand significant human effort, making large-scale adoption impractical. This paper introduces an all-encompassing framework for ability-based knowledge integration, defined by a structured schema, three knowledge sources, two override mechanisms, and a set of guidelines for practical implementation. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first comprehensive framework for ability-based skill integration. We validated the schema's utility through an automatic construction pipeline that incorporated 23 distinct source types. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework outperforms alternative knowledge integration methods when guiding LLMs in prioritizing specific abilities over others. Additionally, the framework significantly reduced hallucinations in open-domain dialogue by nearly half compared to standard inference. As a fully automated, all-inclusive solution, our approach offers a cost-effective alternative to labor-intensive manual overrides, providing a valuable tool for refining LLMs in actual deployments. The proposed framework is accessible at: https://github.com/IBM/ABILITY.

Non-linear interactions between electromagnetic fields (EMF) arise due to vacuum polarization within quantum electrodynamics (QED). Such interactions suggest that non-linear electrodynamics could significantly impact black hole physics. In this study, we examine the connection between thermal dynamics and observable shadows for non-linear charged AdS black holes carrying both electric and magnetic charges. The results indicate that the emergence of a shadow during black hole evolution is directly linked to a turning point in the thermodynamic temperature. Specifically, when a global maximum or minimum temperature is reached, the black hole shrinks until its horizon size matches the radius where the shadow forms. Conversely, global temperature maxima are associated with the formation of shadows, whereas minima are not. These findings suggest that non-linear electrodynamics plays a crucial role in the creation of black hole shadows. Additionally, we observe that for a fixed electric charge, increasing the non-linear parameter $\gamma$ leads to a larger shadow radius. However, when the product of electric and magnetic charges ($Q_e Q_m$) remains constant, the influence of $\gamma$ on the shadow radius depends on the specific charge values: if $Q_e > 0.63$, the shadow radius decreases as $\gamma$ increases; if $Q_e < 0.63$, it increases; and if $Q_e = 0.63$, the radius remains unchanged regardless of $\gamma$. These conclusions hold true for both linear and non-linear electric charges. Finally, we find that the third order of the near horizon expansion for the temperature ($T_{GH}$) and the shadow radius ($r_s$) yields identical results. This work underscores the significance of non-linear electrodynamics in the physics of black hole shadows. The methods presented here may also prove valuable for analyzing other black hole models. Regarding notation, we utilize geometric units where $G=c=k_B=1$ and the electric charge unit is defined as $4\pi\epsilon_0=1$. The non-linear parameter is given by $\gamma = 2/\Lambda^2$. Readers interested in restoring SI units can refer to Appendix A. Our primary goal is to establish a relationship between the shadow radius and temperature for non-linear charged AdS black holes, highlighting how the shadow radius varies with temperature under different physical conditions. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 describes the black hole model and its key properties; Section 3 presents the main findings; and Section 4 offers our conclusions.

We introduce the Wigner distribution (or quantum phase-space distribution) for continuous-variable systems, presenting its representation within optical homodyne tomograms. Utilizing this framework, we mathematically characterize modification distributions of entanglement and the initial distribution of continuous-variable entanglement synchronization as depicted in these tomograms. Through simple illustrative examples, we demonstrate the applicability of these newly defined distributions. Furthermore, we apply these concepts to experimentally verify the existence of synchronization in continuous variables. Finally, we outline the potential utility of the entanglement modification distribution and the initial entanglement synchronization distribution in investigating entanglement dynamics and related phenomena. These applications mirror those of the entanglement concentration distribution in optics, which has been employed to explore entanglement concentration across spatial, temporal, and spectral domains of light fields. The formulation of the entanglement modification distribution within optical tomography could similarly enable the examination of entanglement modification (i.e., entanglement harvesting) between continuous-variable systems in this context. We conclude by addressing the challenge of determining whether an unknown quantum state is genuinely quantum or merely classical using optical homodyne measurements, a problem that remains unresolved in continuous-variable systems. This determination requires calculating the "violation distribution" of the Wigner function, drawing a parallel to how the entanglement modification distribution was derived from the negativity of the density matrix in optical phase-space tomograms. The development of a comparable violation distribution for the Wigner function of continuous variables within their tomograms could facilitate ascertaining entanglement modifications when only tomographic data is available. These applications highlight the significance of defining the entanglement modification distribution and initial entanglement synchronization distribution in the Wigner function of continuous variables and their analysis via optical homodyne tomograms. We finalize by emphasizing that the concept of entanglement modification distribution in optical density matrices can be extended to any quantum system's density matrix, potentially guiding the exploration of entanglement modifications in other quantum systems through their respective distributions.

This work demonstrates that certain classic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ can exhibit biharmonic properties when characterized by the Euclidean classical and semi-classical operators. We analyze these surfaces within the domain of Euclidean biharmonic geometry, emphasizing their unique features and operational mechanisms. Specifically, we prove that biharmonicity defined through Euclidean geometry, via the Euclidean classical operator, is equivalent to a corresponding biharmonicity definition using the Euclidean semi-classical operator. Based on this equivalence, we derive a criterion for Euclidean biharmonicity rooted in the Euclidean classical operator. Furthermore, we construct specific Euclidean hypersurfaces that are biharmonic under this criterion, providing detailed examples of these constructions. Our investigations focus on Euclidean hypersurfaces possessing constant mean curvature, constant scalar curvature, and those defined by the product of the Euclidean classical Laplacian and Euler operator. Ultimately, we establish that Euclidean biharmonicity, as defined by the Euclidean semi-classical operator, implies that these specific hypersurfaces must also be biharmonic under the Euclidean classical operator criterion. Consequently, we conclude that constant mean curvature and constant scalar curvature cannot coexist in Euclidean-invariant biharmonic hypersurfaces. Our analysis also covers Euclidean-invariant surfaces with these constant curvatures that are defined by the Euclidean semi-classical Laplacian and Euler operator.

This study presents an initial measurement of the differential decay rate for the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decay. An analysis of 3.2 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV is performed using events reconstructed via the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+$ and $\bar{B}_s^0\rightarrow \bar{D}_s^{*+}\mu^-$ decay chains. The differential rate as a function of the neutronicity variable is modeled using both polynomial and z-expansion formulations. Through a fit to the data, the most probable form of the differential decay rate aligns with the polynomial expansion up to fourth order or the $z$-expansion with two coefficients per term. Ultimately, the specific form employed to describe the differential decay rate in this study is determined by the coefficient with the largest uncertainty.

We report on acoustic emission (AE) measured during the peeling of an adhesive tape unrolled at constant speed. By analyzing the AE spectrum and waveform, we identified that the cracking sound results from cavitating air, and that the acoustic structure correlates directly with the air cavity shape. Furthermore, dividing the AE spectrum into frequency bands reveals a concealed ordered structure within the apparent noisy spectrum. This order is evident when examining the temporal appearance of specific frequency bands and becomes particularly clear via a spectrogram. Finally, we establish a connection between this concealed order and the air cavity structure.

In 1930/31, Menger introduced the concept of an abstract angle space, considering it a foundational element for developing a theory of topos geometry. He also identified two challenges regarding the existence of such spaces within Euclidean geometry, which he deemed necessary for establishing a topos geometry in that context. Around 1918, Tolles attempted to address these problems but ultimately failed. We will explain the source of these difficulties, which stemmed from an inappropriate definition of the function $\alpha$ used at the time. Furthermore, we will demonstrate that a solution is achievable if one works with a new definition. This adjustment also enables a formulation of the angle space concept for Toeplitz geometry. Finally, it is possible to define an "existence theorem" for these geometries with a revised version of the criterion originally proposed by Menger. However, true solutions to the problems he formulated require adopting a new criterion for the axioms of topology. Under these circumstances, one can establish an existence theorem for Euclidean geometry as early as 1918 and, with minor modifications, for Toeplitz geometry from around 1914. These outcomes signify that certain mathematical goals were feasible back then, had the appropriate definitions been selected. Such findings do not imply that mathematicians of that era were incapable of these tasks; rather, it simply means the necessary definitions had not yet been developed. This conclusion aligns perfectly with Menger's own viewpoint on the introduction of new concepts, as expressed in the preamble of his 1930 paper [5]. Following this analysis, we will present the revised definitions required to resolve the issues Menger raised in his 1930/31 works. Our approach begins with a examination of the developments in this field prior to 1930.

This work introduces Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC), a technique designed to neutralize the impact of geometric transformations—such as rotation, scaling, and translation—on point cloud structures without compromising structural details. First, we conduct comprehensive analyses of existing methods, identifying their limitations and deriving a unified mathematical framework. Within this framework, we systematically examine various smoothing techniques to select the most effective one for TPC. Second, we propose a novel method called Rotation-Coordinate Smoothing (RCS) to replace a weakness in the current state-of-the-art, Linear Transformation Smoothing (LTS), specifically addressing affine distortions. Third, we develop a regularisation term as a regularised version of LTS, demonstrating through experiments that RTPC (Regularised Transformation-Unique Point Cloud) and LTS share identical structural representations under any affine transformation, while RTPC offers an orthogonal representation relative to RTPC. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of TPC using unsupervised techniques, demonstrating its utility in outlier detection, anomaly identification, and other downstream applications. Our source code is accessible at: https://github.com/Xiaoyu-1999/TPC.

This paper presents a geometric framework for evaluating semantic properties of algorithms through a unified geometric language. Unlike traditional semantic analyses, which are typically tailored to specific properties like equivalence or inclusion, our approach constructs a lattice of programs and three significant sub lattices: contexts, properties, and algorithms. These constructions are achieved via a series of functors operating within the category of ordered sets and monotone functions. Leveraging this geometric perspective, we formally define and compute key semantic properties, including observational properties (such as equivalence, inclusion, and orthogonality), algorithmic properties (like refinement and composition), and meta properties (such as soundness, completeness, and ideality). To demonstrate the practical application of this framework, we developed an automated tool called MetaProperty, which validates meta properties of algorithmic properties across various programs. The outcomes reveal that common meta properties do not always hold, offering insights into the limitations of specific program semantics. Ultimately, this geometric framework serves as a valuable meta property analyzer for algorithmic properties, supporting the validation of semantic meta properties in alternative frameworks. As a meta property validator, our framework complements existing verification systems by assessing their meta properties, thereby facilitating the derivation of new semantic properties for algorithms. Furthermore, the framework acts as a meta property validator for meta programming languages, a concept explored in detail later in this document. All constructions and proofs are implemented in the Homology, Triangulation and Verification (HoVer) library for Coq, with access details provided at https://github.com/verifhover/hover. The source code for this paper and the MetaProperty tool are available at https://github.com/shivang987/GEM.

This paper presents a novel approach to linking Serre weights with modular forms for GL_2, grounded in Kummer theory. Unlike conventional methods, this approach does not rely on p-adic Hodge theory. Utilizing this new framework, we demonstrate a deterministic criterion for a Serre weight to be clear, thereby establishing that such weights are predominantly deformable. As a byproduct of our methodology, we provide a deterministic characterization of clear serre weights that is entirely based on residue characteristics and Dynkin diagrams, requiring no additional number theoretic inputs. Through an application of this characterization, we are able to refine recent findings by Allen, Evans, and Herzig regarding the clarity of Serre weights. Furthermore, in collaboration with S. Morra, our framework enables the derivation of an effective lower bound for the proportion of clear serre weights within families of simple algebraic groups.

This study introduces a form of post-yield damage detection for fiber-reinforced composites through self-sensing electrical impedance tomography (EIT), paired with a novel genetic algorithm-based damage localization strategy. For carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminates, this approach offers a cost-effective, real-time method for identifying both the onset and specific location of inter-fiber delaminations post-yielding. A single-pulse electrical transient measurement technique is employed to enhance the physical robustness of the EIT reconstruction, utilizing a greedy algorithm for initial damage detection. Subsequently, a customized genetic algorithm refines the process to precisely determine inter-fiber delamination sizes. The proposed method is validated against manually introduced delaminations in a [02/902]s CFEP laminate and natural delaminations arising from impact loads on a [0/+45n/90n]s CF/Glass hybrid laminate. Results confirm that this combination of EIT and genetic algorithms can accurately detect inter-fiber delaminations as small as 2.54 cm (1 inch) in size. Furthermore, the system effectively distinguishes between multiple delaminations with varying dimensions and those occurring on opposite sides of the same impact zone. This contactless, real-time damage forming detection via electrical transient techniques holds significant value for enabling self-monitoring and self-diagnostic capabilities in advanced carbon fiber composites used for high-value, safety-critical applications. Our results indicate that for this specific space, the volume-based metric yields a superior representation when utilizing the direct-product tensor. Concluding with a table that summarizes the key properties of various representation methods for Euclidean spaces, this work offers guidance on selecting the most appropriate tensor approach for given requirements. High-dimensional matrix inversion is crucial in fields like machine learning, statistics, and signal processing. While low-dimensional inversion is typically solved via numerical methods such as Cholesky or Cayley-Hamilton expansions, these approaches do not scale well to higher dimensions. Recently, Cohen and Nguyen (2020) introduced a Cayley-based technique achieving O(d3/log(d)) complexity and a higher-order method reaching O(d2.75/polylog(d)), both designed for hardware acceleration. However, the elevated order method relies on at least three Cayley expansions per iteration, making it significantly more computation-heavy per step than the Cayley-based approach. This work presents a novel elevated order algorithm with complexity O(d2.75/polylog(d)), generalizing the method from Cohen and Nguyen (2020). Although this new technique does not alter the fundamental d3 complexity per dimension, it delivers a substantial practical speedup. Specifically, for a dimension of d=10,000, the complexity improves from 108 to approximately 106.25 (a factor of ~15,849), and for d=100,000, it drops from 1015 to roughly 1012.37 (a factor of ~292,657). Empirical results confirm these theoretical gains, demonstrating a 20x speedup for d=10,000 and a 100x speedup for d=100,000. These findings indicate that the generalized elevated order method is highly effective for large-scale inversion tasks, always outperforming both the Cayley and elevated order techniques from Cohen and Nguyen (2020). The implementation, named REVO (Rapid Elevated Order Inversion for High-Dimensional Matrices), is available at https://github.com/ahughey1/generalized_elevated_order_inversion. This article was previously preprinted at arXiv:10.48.2020.2020.05.01.

Contextual learning agents operate within a setting where an agent, or a team of agents, selects actions based on contextual inputs, with the goal of maximizing rewards determined by a linear function of the context. This paper examines the learning algorithm of a team of linear contextual agents, whose contexts are determined independently and identically according to a potentially unknown linear model. Specifically, we address the challenge of optimizing these agents' selections to maximize rewards, in a scenario where contexts are determined independently by a logit-normal distribution and are private to each agent. We introduce a novel algorithm, ReLeCoL (Regularized Low-rank Contextion), a non-asynchronous method that does not require contexts to be ordered. This algorithm achieves an asymptotically optimal lower bound of $O(\log(n))$ for the regret over a polynomial number of steps $n$. The proposed method extends beyond logit-normal distributions, remaining effective under broader distributions such as those found in side-information settings. Furthermore, ReLeCoL is distribution-free and distribution-agnostic, requiring no knowledge of the context distribution's parameters a priori. Additionally, the algorithm operates without needing an explicit dictionary of contexts or their historical records. Numerical experiments conducted on real-world data from online advertising and job recruitment demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy. These experiments also highlight the algorithm's robustness when the assumed context distribution differs from the actual distribution and when the low-rank assumption of the weight vector is only approximately satisfied. Crucially, these experiments confirm that the algorithm's performance does not depend on knowing the specific context distribution, nor does it require the low-rank structure of the context distribution's precision matrix. Finally, we generalize this finding to an infinite-dimensional context space, establishing that the performance relies solely on the low-rank nature of the context space's precision matrix. An open-access implementation of ReLeCoL is available at https://github.com/ravinder1994/ReLeCoL-. We conclude by discussing potential future research directions. The core contributions of this work are that the agent(s) do not need to know the specific context distribution (neither its low-rank structure nor its mean vector), and in multi-agent systems, the contexts of other agents do not need to be drawn from the same distribution as the main agent's contexts. Furthermore, the agent(s) are not required to know the lower bound of the Lipschitz constant of the reward function associated with the context distribution. These results signify that the agent(s) do not require any prior knowledge of the context distribution.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) acts as a source of turbulence in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. However, VSI-driven gas motions induce vertical expansions that can trigger dust condensation in outer disk zones, which in turn may dampen these motions and potentially halt the instability. In this work, we first linearly analyze how dust condensation influences VSI growth rates within dust-rich regions. Subsequently, using linear and linear-hybrid simulations followed by non-linear simulations, we investigate the linear growth rates and overall stability of the VSI in both dust-poor and dust-rich zones, accounting for dust condensation effects. Our results indicate that linear growth occurs in dust-rich regions only when the midplane temperature ($T_m$) falls below approximately 140 K. Furthermore, once dust condensation is triggered by VSI-induced gas motions, it significantly suppresses the instability's growth rate; for instance, at a midplane temperature of 80 K, the growth rate decreases by a factor of two. In these regions, dust condensation acts as a damping mechanism, damping vertical oscillations of the gas even when they exceed the sound speed. While dust condensation strongly suppresses VSI growth rates linearly and dampens oscillations non-linearly, our non-linear simulations show that instability still occurs in dust-poor outer zones. These motions induce vertical oscillations that periodically trigger condensation in the adjacent dust-rich midplane, though this damping effect does not prevent non-linear non-stationary gas motions in those areas. Consequently, VSI-driven flows between dust-poor and dust-rich zones could drive significant mixing, potentially altering assumptions about dust distribution used in planet formation models. Additional linear simulations were conducted on a grid with a z-direction resolution of 0.05 H, where H represents the local scale height.

This study tackles the challenge of Federated Learning (FL) arising from data distributions that are both independent and skewed across clients. While gradient-descent based methods like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) struggle to converge effectively under such "independent and heavy-tailed" distributions, we introduce Random Stroll (RS) as an alternative optimization algorithm for FS. Theoretically, we establish convergence rates for both SGD and RS under independent but heavy-tailed data distributions. Specifically, the convergence rate for RS is linearly related to the dimension, whereas the rate for gradient-descent methods is quadratically related. Simulation results confirm that RS outperforms SGD, particularly when clients exhibit significant data distribution skewness. To address the high communication costs associated with RS, we propose a variant called Adaptive Random Stroll (ARS), which utilizes a subspace derived from the Hessian of the global loss function. Under mild conditions, ARS achieves the same optimal rate as RS without requiring explicit Hessian computation or storage. Comparative simulations between RS, ARS, and standard descent methods demonstrate that RS and its variant AS significantly surpass conventional optimization approaches in terms of communication efficiency.

Consistency regularization is a prominent approach for unlabeled data within deep learning-based medical image segmentation. This study introduces a new consistency regularization method that effectively combines adversarial training and consistency regularization to enhance the robustness of segmentation networks against perturbations in both images and latent representations. Specifically, the algorithm ensures that the segmentation of an unlabeled adversarially perturbed image remains consistent with the segmentation of the same image when subjected to a consistency constraint. Additionally, it guarantees alignment between the segmentation of the adversarially perturbed image and that of the original image under a distributional constraint. To achieve this, we employ an adversarial optimization technique for the former and a simple consistency constraint for the latter. We evaluated our approach on two public datasets, ACDC and PaIGAN. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing consistency-based and adversarial-based techniques in both segmentation performance and robustness. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrally incorporate adversarial training and consistency regularization—typically considered conflicting strategies—to improve the robustness of segmentation networks against perturbations in both inputs and latent variables for unlabeled data. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Ahmed-Elgharib-87/CR-Adversary-MSC.

Although the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with advanced information technology systems has yielded substantial benefits, it has simultaneously amplified the exposure and potential consequences of security and privacy vulnerabilities. The Internet of Vehicles (IoV), a core component of the smart IoV, is particularly susceptible to these issues. In parallel, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for addressing privacy and security concerns within the IoV. Concurrently, Blockchain technology has gained significant traction due to its inherent characteristics of decentralization, immutability, and traceability, which are particularly advantageous for IoV applications.
